sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
We have only recent data for Hamburg's garages, so there is no city trend yet; the figures below are for weekdays in August and September 2026.

Hamburg is reducing the car's place in the centre gradually and pricing the street up. In 2020 it presented plans to make the Jungfernstieg largely car-free, leaving it to buses, deliveries and bikes [0], and in 2023 the Senate set a goal of 80% of trips on foot, by bike or by public transport by 2030 [2]. In 2026 street parking became dearer for the first time since 2022: €4.00 an hour in the city-centre zone, up from €3.50, with residents' permits rising to €70 [3]. Electric cars still park free at meters, but that exemption is due to end at the close of 2026 [4]. The city is also testing new ways of managing parking: checking parking rights by number plate with scan cars instead of paper tickets [5], and letting residents and visitors book supermarket car parks overnight [6]. Park-and-ride became paid almost everywhere by the end of 2019, while the annual card was halved to €100 [1]. Public transport is busy, with more than 1.1 billion journeys expected in 2024 [15], and cruise passengers reached a record 1.3 million [16].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
The biggest new car park is not in the old centre but in HafenCity. Westfield Hamburg-Überseequartier opened in April 2025 [7] with about 2,500 spaces, dynamic pricing capped at €39 a day [8] and ticketless entry by plate recognition [9]. In our data the nearby Überseequartier Nord garage, run by Contipark, is almost empty on weekdays (8%). In the old town, parking is giving way to housing: the Gröninger Hof car park is to become 90 subsidised flats [10]. The Alsterhaus department store kept trading through its owner's 2024 insolvency [11].

Charging has moved into garages quickly. E.ON opened 18 fast chargers on the seventh deck of the new MediaMarkt garage on Mönckebergstraße [12], APCOA made Hamburg the focus of its 2025 roll-out with 55 points in four garages [13], and the city counted 5,063 public charging points in April 2026, 40% more than a year earlier [14].

sections.title: Operators, location, price and use
sections.text:
Hamburg has no dominant garage operator. APCOA has the most sites in our research set (about 15, a third of its spaces within a kilometre of the Jungfernstieg), followed by Sprinkenhof, whose garages are mostly central and priced well above their neighbours, and Contipark, whose garages are mostly outside the centre and cheap (typically €1.65 an hour). Q-Park's City-Parkhaus is the largest central garage and the cheapest, at about €2 an hour, roughly a third below its neighbours. Shopping centres such as the Alstertal-Einkaufszentrum and the Phoenix-Center run their own car parks.

Price and use fall together with distance from the centre. Within a kilometre of the Jungfernstieg, garages typically charge €4.50 an hour and €40 a day, above the new street rate, and are about 40% occupied on weekdays. The busiest are APCOA's Alter Wall/Bucerius Passage garage (66%) and the Marriott garage (65%); the City-Parkhaus stands at 46%. Further out the picture changes completely: the big suburban shopping-centre car parks, at around €1.50 an hour or €15 a day, are only 7–26% full on weekdays (Alstertal 22–26%, Phoenix-Center 12%, CCB Billstedt 10–13%, Harburg Carrée 7%). Hamburg's dearest garages are its fullest because they are the central ones.
